source_read: PDF pp. 1–6 (PDFs/Methamphetamine/McKetin_2020_ContributionMethamphetamineUseCrime.pdf), all pages; Table 1 and Fig. 1 checked on pages rendered at 110 dpi, and Fig. 1's bars measured at 300 dpi against the gridlines. The online supplement (Tables S1–S3) is not available and was not read. Step 1 (blind extraction) not run this round, per the round brief.

design.note: Prospective cohort is right: a within-person analysis of four one-month panels (baseline, 3 months, 1 year, 3 years) from the MATES cohort (pp. 2–3). The can_establish and cannot_establish sentences fit the design. One refinement for both and for comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: the claim that stable characteristics are removed by the design holds for the fixed-effects estimator; because the abstract and methods describe the estimator ambiguously (reporting issue 0), 'designed to remove' would be more exact.

key_findings.note: p. 2, 2.1, 1st paragraph (starts at the foot of the left column and continues in the right): 400 people entering community-based treatment in Sydney and Brisbane and 101 in Sydney not in treatment (needle and syringe programmes, outreach) who screened positive for dependence; interviews at baseline, 3 months, 1 year and 3 years; recruitment 2006 and 2007, follow-up 2006 to 2010; face-to-face or by phone; the four entry criteria as listed.
p. 2, 2.1, 2nd paragraph: 17, 14 and 1 excluded; 469 aged 16–57; 379 (81%), 357 (76%) and 315 (67%); seven missing crime responses; 1518, 1514 and 1513 months. The note's 484 (501 − 17) is right.

pp. 2–3, 2.1.1.1 to 2.1.1.3: the OTI crime scale with four crime types and five frequency categories; days of methamphetamine use in the past four weeks, all routes and main form; days of heroin, cocaine, ecstasy, hallucinogens, cannabis, alcohol and tobacco use (top of p. 3); age, net fortnightly income, unemployment and unstable housing; hair toxicology in 83 people, 6% false reports of abstinence (p. 2). 'Coded any against none' is stated in 2.1.2 (p. 3).

p. 3, 2.1.2, and Table 1 notes a and b: as stated. Age is also a time-varying covariate in both adjusted models (Table 1 notes a and b; abstract), although the list in 2.1.2 omits it; adding 'and age' to the covariate list would make the finding complete.
p. 3, 3.1, 1st paragraph (starts at the foot of the left column): every figure as stated, from mean age 31.6 (SD 8.1) to base 31% and powder 8%.

p. 3, 3.1, 2nd paragraph: every figure as stated, including rs 0.08–0.40, AUD500 (IQR 420–800), 68% and 15% of months. '10% of participants used at every interview' renders the paper's 'at all follow-ups'.
p. 3, 3.1, 3rd paragraph: 52%, 45%, 25% and 22% of people; 41%, 24%, 21%, 10% and 9% of months. Table 1 reproduces the month shares (619, 363, 322, 153 and 132 of 1,520 months; editors' arithmetic).
Table 1 counts as stated. I recomputed every percentage: only 104 of 593 (17.5%) is printed outside rounding (17); the others round correctly.

Table 1 (rendered page): every odds ratio, interval and p value as stated, including the stray full stop in '5.3.'. Geometric midpoints recomputed (for example √(8.5 × 20.6) = 13.2; √(1.5 × 8.0) = 3.5 against 3.4; √(0.8 × 3.3) = 1.6 against 1.7, within the rounding of the limits), and the Model 2 p values agree with their intervals (fraud z about 1.47, p about 0.14 against 0.158; violent crime z about 2.87, p about 0.004 against 0.005).

p. 3, 3.2, 2nd paragraph: heroin (dealing, property crime, fraud), cannabis (dealing, fraud), heavier alcohol use non-significant for violent crime, no socio-economic indicator significant, all referred to Table S2.

3.2, 3rd paragraph (begins on p. 3 and ends on p. 4 with the reference to Table S3); Fig. 1 (p. 4). My own measurement of the bars at 300 dpi: any crime 18.1, 48.3 and 71.2%; dealing 6.2, 27.1 and 53.2; fraud 5.1, 12.3 and 16.3; property crime 7.1, 26.2 and 39.2; violent crime 3.2, 9.3 and 19.2. The card's readings agree to the nearest point.

p. 4, Discussion, 1st paragraph ('robust evidence', large increase, the time-varying controls showing the increase could not be accounted for) and 3rd paragraph (violent crime not only a consequence of pre-existing risk; instrumental against expressive violence).

p. 5, 4.1, 1st to 3rd paragraphs: as stated, including the authors' argument that crime leading to more use is unlikely and that the association more likely reflects desisting from crime during abstinence.

key_findings.correction: The author list includes McKetin, Boden and Foulds, three of the four authors of the Christchurch birth-cohort study of violence (Foulds et al., 2020; the fourth, Newton-Howes, is not an author of this paper), which the introduction cites.
key_findings.note: Introduction, 3rd paragraph (p. 2) confirms the earlier hostility and psychosis analyses (2013b, 2014); the introduction cites Foulds et al. (2020) in its 1st paragraph (p. 1) and 2nd paragraph (p. 2). The reference list (p. 6) shows that Foulds et al. (2020) has four authors, so 'the authors of' overstates. The note is right that this paper does not say which cohort the 2013b and 2014 analyses used.

reporting_issues.note: Abstract, Methods (p. 1): odds ratios extracted from a random-intercept logistic model; 2.1.2 (p. 3): random-effects xtlogit models with a random intercept, and the fixed-effects option used for the within-person effect. Stata's xtlogit fits either a random-effects or a conditional fixed-effects model, so the two descriptions name different estimators. No count of contributing participants is given anywhere. The consequence is correctly stated.

p. 3, 3.2, 1st paragraph (13.2 times more likely); p. 4, Discussion, 1st paragraph (five times more likely). The same risk-ratio reading is applied to the adjusted estimates in 3.2, 2nd paragraph (five to six times for property crime and dealing, 3.4 times for violent crime), which the issue could add. Editors' arithmetic recomputed: 55.6/17.5 = 3.2; for violent crime the raw risk ratio is 3.8 and the raw odds ratio 4.2.
Abstract (p. 1): effects were dose related; Fig. 1 (p. 4) prints no values or intervals; 3.2, 3rd paragraph refers the adjusted gradient to Table S3.
p. 3, 3.2, 3rd paragraph: 16 or more days compared with 0–15 days; 2.1.2: 1–15 and 16+ days against no use; Fig. 1 shows three categories.
Table 1 column headers n = 593 and n = 927 (1,520 months) against 1,513–1,518 analysed months (p. 2); 17 printed for 17.5; my Fig. 1 reading of the no-use bar for any crime is 18.1%.
p. 2: the first sentence of 2.1 gives 469 as the number meeting DSM-IV criteria, while the 2nd paragraph's exclusions give 484 meeting them.
p. 5: the funding section names the NHMRC (Project Grant 350974) and the Department of Health and Ageing, and the role-of-funding-source statement declares nothing.

instrument.note: ROBINS-E fits an observational study of an exposure; the seven domains are the instrument's and use its vocabulary.

domains.note: Some concerns is defensible. A stricter reader could rate it high, because treatment entry and receipt and imprisonment, which plausibly change both use and crime from month to month, are not measured, and reverse causation within the month cannot be excluded. That would not change the overall judgment.
Self-reported days of use, validated only in a subsample of the parent cohort (p. 2).

The point that only people whose crime status changed contribute to a fixed-effects estimate concerns the effective sample more than selection bias; it is a fair flag beside the treatment-entry selection.
81%, 76% and 67% retained (p. 2); no comparison of those retained and lost.
Same-interview self-report of use and crime, uncorroborated.
Exploratory and not pre-registered (p. 3); full and dose models only in the supplement.

overall.note: High. Some concerns in every domain, several pointing the same way (same-interview self-report, unmeasured changes around treatment entry and imprisonment, reverse causation within the month), fit ROBINS-E's rule that concerns in several domains can substantially lower confidence, and the overall is not less severe than any domain (METHODS 5.3). The reasoning's restriction on use (within-person adjusted associations in people with dependence; not causal, not recreational use, not recorded offending) is what the paper supports.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. The six gaps are on the stated pages: 'likely social consequence' (p. 1), 'robust evidence' and 'could not be accounted for' (p. 4), 'times more likely' (pp. 3–4), 'dose related' resting on unadjusted pooled percentages, and the restriction to dependent people stated only in the limitations (p. 5). Not severe, because the authors state the direction problem, the self-report and the restriction themselves. One fix in results_show and in exposure.polysubstance: 'adjustment for other substance use roughly halved the estimates' is loose; from Model 1 to Model 2 the odds ratios fell by 35% to 63% (any crime 10.5 to 4.7, dealing 15.8 to 5.9, fraud 2.8 to 1.7, property crime 8.4 to 5.5, violent crime 5.3 to 3.4), so 'by a third to nearly two-thirds' is exact.

missed: funding.affiliations_note says that two authors (McKetin, Foulds) of the 2019 meta-analysis are authors here. The reference list (p. 6) shows four: McKetin, Foulds, Farrell and Degenhardt. The claim's statement and anchor 10 already say four; the card should match.

Fig. 1's caption (p. 4) labels the bars 'percentage of participants reporting crime in the past month', but the no-use bars reproduce Table 1's shares of months (violent crime 3.2%, any crime about 18%), so the unit is months. A minor reporting issue worth adding, because the card and the violence claim cite the bars as shares of months.

The 2014 MATES paper that the introduction (p. 2) describes as an analysis of hostility is titled, in the reference list (p. 6), 'Does methamphetamine use increase violent behaviour? Evidence from a prospective longitudinal study' (Addiction 109, 798–806). The replication timeline could give the title, because the violence claim counts that paper as a violence study inside the review's pooled estimate.

Several fields (can_establish, comparison.unmeasured_premorbid, the reasoning) state that the design removes stable confounding. That holds for the fixed-effects estimator, which the methods name, but not for the random-intercept model the abstract names (reporting issue 0); 'designed to remove' would be more exact.
